Fetal Echo Project · Unit D1 · Detect tier · v0.2

The normal heart in five views

Verified content.

You will be able to

  • Perform the five-plane sweep in order and say what each plane must show.
  • Set up the machine for a cardiac screen.
  • Give the normal values for heart size, axis and rate, and the rates that need referral.
  • List the criteria that make a four-chamber view normal.
  • Confirm normal outflow tracts and a normal three-vessel-and-trachea view.

Why five views

A screening scan does not need to name the lesion. It needs to answer one question reliably: is this heart normal? The five-view sweep is the shortest route to that answer.

Congenital heart disease affects about 8 in every 1000 live births, and fewer than half of cardiac anomalies are found before birth.1,2

Most detectable heart disease occurs in pregnancies with no risk factor at all. That is why the routine scan matters more than the referral list.3

Some lesions, such as transposition and coarctation, may show nothing in the four-chamber plane. Adding the outflow-tract and great-vessel views raises detection above the four-chamber view alone.4,5,6

The examination should include situs, the four-chamber view, and the outflow-tract and great-vessel views, ideally between 18 and 22 weeks.7,8

Set up before you scan

Use the highest transducer frequency that still penetrates. Harmonic imaging helps when the abdominal wall is thick and in the third trimester.9,10

Choose the cardiac preset: high frame rate, more contrast, low persistence, a single focal zone and a narrow sector.11

Zoom until the heart fills a third to a half of the screen. Use cine-loop to watch the valves through the whole cycle.12,13

Store stills and clips of each view so the examination can be reviewed later.14

The sweep

The examination is one continuous transverse sweep towards the fetal head through five planes: upper abdomen, four-chamber view, left ventricular outflow tract, right ventricular outflow tract with the three-vessel view, and the three-vessel-and-trachea view.15,16,17

The upper planes are a continuum, not fixed pictures. They are judged more reliably live or on a clip than from stills.18

If the fetus is lying badly, take more time or bring the patient back.19

Plane I: left, right and situs

First work out which side of the fetus is left and which is right from its position in the uterus. Only then confirm that stomach and heart are both on the left.20

At the level of the abdominal circumference: stomach on the left, descending aorta to the left of the spine, inferior vena cava to the right.21

Normal abdominal situs stands in for normal atrial arrangement. If heart or stomach is not on the left, suspect a situs abnormality.22,23

Plane II: size, position, axis, rate

A normal heart is no larger than a third of the chest area.24

It lies mainly in the left chest with its axis pointing left at about 45 degrees, 20 degrees either way. You can judge axis and position even when the rest of the view is poor.25,26

An abnormal axis raises the chance of a heart defect, especially of the outflow tracts. A heart that is pushed out of place points to something beside it: diaphragmatic hernia, a lung mass, or a small or absent lung.27,28

Rate is 120 to 160 beats per minute and regular. Occasional ectopic beats are common and usually harmless. Refer if they are frequent or the rhythm stays irregular for more than a week or two.29,30,31

A brief slow rate from probe pressure is normal. A rate that stays at 110 or below, or at 180 or above, needs specialist assessment.32,33

Plane II: the four-chamber criteria

Seeing four chambers is not the same as a normal four-chamber view. The view is judged against specific criteria.34

Atria: similar in size, foramen ovale flap moving in the left atrium, septum primum present. Where you can, show at least one pulmonary vein entering the left atrium.35,36

Ventricles: similar in size, walls not thick. The moderator band marks the right ventricle; the smooth left ventricle forms the apex.37,38

One ventricle clearly smaller than the other in mid-pregnancy is not a variant. Think of coarctation, an evolving hypoplastic left heart, and anomalous pulmonary veins.38

Septum: follow it from apex to crux. It is best seen with the beam at right angles; with the beam along the septum, drop-out can fake a defect near the crux.39,40

Valves: two, opening separately and freely, with the tricuspid attached slightly nearer the apex than the mitral. Loss of that offset is a key sign of atrioventricular septal defect.41

A thin rim of pericardial fluid, up to 2 mm, is normal.42

Plane III: left ventricular outflow tract

A vessel leaves the left ventricle. Its front wall runs straight on from the ventricular septum, and it does not divide. The valve is thin and opens freely.43,44,45

This view shows outlet septal defects and conotruncal and aortic valve problems that the four-chamber view hides.46

Plane IV: right ventricular outflow tract and three vessels

A vessel leaves the right ventricle, crosses in front of the aorta almost at a right angle, and divides after a short course. It is usually slightly larger than the aorta. Its valve is thin and opens freely.43,47,48

At the least, the two great arteries should be about the same size. A clear difference needs further assessment.49

Three vessels in a line: pulmonary artery, aorta, superior vena cava, from left to right and from front to back, each smaller than the one before. Check number, size, alignment and arrangement.50

Transposition, tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, common arterial trunk and pulmonary atresia with a septal defect can all pass the four-chamber view. They typically fail this one.51

Plane V: three vessels and trachea

The ductal arch and the aortic arch both pass to the left of the trachea and meet in a V. The two arches are similar in size. The trachea is a bright ring around a small dark centre.52,53,54

This is the view for the arch: coarctation, right arch, double arch, vascular rings and an aberrant right subclavian artery.55,56

Colour Doppler

Colour is not mandatory for screening but is encouraged once you are competent with it.57

Keep the colour box small and over the area of interest. Set the scale to about 50 to 70 cm/s for the heart and arteries, and about 15 to 25 cm/s for veins.58,59

Normal colour shows forward flow through all four valves and both arches. It makes the V easier to see and exposes leaking valves and reversed flow in an arch.60

When the screen is not normal

Any fetus with a suspected abnormality on screening should have a fetal echocardiogram.61

About half of missed diagnoses in one study came from views that did not meet technical standards, and nearly a third from not recognising the abnormality on an adequate view. Both are trainable.62
